record.title: A preprint reports graph-format sensitivity and an adaptive reasoning scaffold for graph algorithms
record.summary: A September 10 preprint introduces GT Bench, a synthetic evaluation of 24 classical graph problems across four textual/structural representations, and reports that the best input representation varies with graph and task structure. Its Graph Theory Agent (GTA) adds learned representation selection and plan/decompose scaffolding around a frozen executor. On the paper’s reported Phi-4 setting, accuracy rises from 53.5% to 69.1% on the easy split and 33.0% to 41.5% on the hard split; the authors also report transfer to other executors and benchmarks. These are author-reported results, not independently reproduced here. The abstract says 44 task–structure settings while Appendix C describes 43 reported settings.
organizations: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors introduce GT Bench with 24 graph problems and over 100,000 examples represented as natural language, structured language, adjacency lists and adjacency matrices; the abstract reports 44 task–structure settings.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports large task-dependent representation effects; for sparse-graph connectivity, reported accuracy ranges from 60.5% to 89.1% across formats.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: With Phi-4 as the executor, the authors report GTA raises accuracy from 53.5% to 69.1% on GT-E and 33.0% to 41.5% on GT-H; Table 14 reports transfer to GPT-4o-mini, GPT-4o and DeepSeek-R1 executors.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper’s reported gains have not been independently reproduced in this activation; Appendix C says it reports 43 task–structure settings, not the abstract’s 44.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction of GT Bench generation, model prompts, or GTA scores was performed.
The abstract reports 44 task–structure settings but Appendix C reports 43.
Generalization beyond synthetic graph tasks and the cost-effectiveness of GTA in operational workloads remain untested here.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported effects hold, graph encoding becomes a practical evaluation and interface variable, and a controller around a frozen executor improves multi-step graph tasks without changing base-model weights. That can affect research and benchmarking choices across structured reasoning, but evidence is a single synthetic benchmark paper with no independent reproduction, so consequence is notable rather than field-shifting.
limitations: Author-reported preprint results only; no independent reproduction, artifact audit or live execution was performed.
The abstract states 44 task–structure settings, while Appendix C describes 43 reported settings; the discrepancy is unresolved.
The paper’s representation sweeps use a single inference run per configuration; the paper says targeted analyses average three runs.
Evaluation is on generated graph problems. Transfer to deployed graph workflows, domain-specific graphs, and materially different graph sizes remains unestablished.
The reported GTA accuracy gains come with additional tokens and cost: Table 15 reports $1.11 versus $0.20 for direct Phi-4 prompting on the stated sample and pricing.
organizations: Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence
brief.summary: A September 10 preprint introduces GT Bench, a synthetic evaluation of 24 classical graph problems across four textual/structural representations, and reports that the best input representation varies with graph and task structure. Its Graph Theory Agent (GTA) adds learned representation selection and plan/decompose scaffolding around a frozen executor. On the paper’s reported Phi-4 setting, accuracy rises from 53.5% to 69.1% on the easy split and 33.0% to 41.5% on the hard split; the authors also report transfer to other executors and benchmarks. These are author-reported results, not independently reproduced here. The abstract says 44 task–structure settings while Appendix C describes 43 reported settings.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report representation-dependent scores across 24 graph problems, a Phi-4 increase of 15.6 percentage points on GT-E and 8.5 points on GT-H, plus transfer results on other executor models. They also report GTA token cost of $1.11 versus $0.20 for direct Phi-4 prompting on 600 mixed instances at the paper’s stated token prices.
technical.demonstrated_result: The public preprint and its reported evaluation tables are accessible. the research desk did not execute the code or reproduce the accuracy/cost figures; technical performance remains author-reported.
technical.mechanism: A learned selector chooses a graph representation; a plan/decompose scaffold breaks algorithmic tasks into steps for a frozen executor LLM. The paper also studies a training-free heuristic selector and a learned selector/decomposer, with the decomposer trained using supervised fine-tuning and preference optimization.
technical.regime: Author-run synthetic GT Bench evaluations: 24 classical graph problems, over 100,000 examples, four representations, easy/hard splits, and several executor LLMs. Transfer is also reported on GraCoRe and NLGraph. Representation sweeps use one inference run per configuration at temperature 0.01; targeted analyses average three runs with standard deviations. No independent replication or real-world graph-task transfer was performed here.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares direct prompting and eight prompting/agent baselines. Table 9 attributes a 7.0 point GT-E increment to decomposition over the selector-only setup. Comparisons and task distributions are author-defined and are not an independent matched replication.

brief.title: A preprint reports graph-format sensitivity and an adaptive reasoning scaffold for graph algorithms
brief.why_it_matters: If replicated, the result suggests that how a graph is encoded can materially affect language-model algorithmic reasoning, and that a lightweight controller around an unchanged model can exploit this sensitivity. It could shift benchmark design and prompt/interface choices for structured reasoning. Current evidence is one author-run preprint evaluation; the size of the gains outside its synthetic graph tasks remains unknown.
